title: 2 Samuel 13:15–22
context: After the assault, Amnon’s desire turns to hatred, and he has Tamar thrown out and the door bolted behind her. Tamar mourns publicly, tearing her royal garment and putting ashes on her head. Absalom tells her to be quiet and takes her into his house, where she remains desolate. David is very angry but takes no action, a real failure of justice, while Absalom silently hates Amnon. Both traditions honor Tamar’s dignity and grief and read the passage as shared ground about sin’s consequences in David’s house.

verses.text: Then Amnon hated her with exceedingly great hatred; for the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. Amnon said to her, “Arise, be gone!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amnon then hates Tamar with a hatred greater than his former ‘love,’ and orders her out. His desire reveals itself as contempt.

Arminian readers see that what Amnon called love was selfish desire, now exposed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The sudden reversal shows the emptiness of Amnon’s passion. He treats Tamar as disposable.

Reformed readers see sin’s self-destructive nature and its cruelty to others. Both traditions read this as shared ground and with full sympathy for Tamar, who is wronged twice over.

verses.text: She said to him, “Not so, because this great wrong in sending me away is worse than the other that you did to me!” But he would not listen to her.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar protests that sending her away is a greater wrong than what he has already done. He again refuses to listen.

Arminian readers see her continuing to speak for justice and her future, with remarkable courage.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tamar understands that being cast out would compound her shame and loss. Her protest is reasoned.

Reformed readers honor her voice once more. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that Amnon’s refusal to listen marks both of his wrongs against her.

verses.text: Then he called his servant who ministered to him, and said, “Now put this woman out from me, and bolt the door after her.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amnon calls his servant to put ‘this woman’ out and bolt the door. He refuses even to name her.

Arminian readers see deliberate humiliation added to the harm. Amnon compounds his crime by casting her out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Amnon speaks of Tamar with contempt. The bolted door seals his rejection.

Reformed readers see the hardness of a heart given over to sin. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground, recognizing the cruelty of treating a wronged sister as an object to be removed.

verses.text: She had a garment of various colors on her, for the king’s daughters who were virgins dressed in such robes. Then his servant brought her out and bolted the door after her.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar wears a garment of various colors, worn by the king’s virgin daughters, and the servant puts her out and bolts the door. Her royal dignity is noted.

Arminian readers see the narrator honoring Tamar’s status even as she is cast out.
verses.reformedNotes:
The same phrase describes Joseph’s robe in Genesis 37:3. Both garments mark honor that others violate.

Reformed readers see the narrator’s sympathy with Tamar. Both traditions read this as shared ground and decline to press the parallel further.

verses.text: Tamar put ashes on her head, and tore her garment of various colors that was on her; and she laid her hand on her head and went her way, crying aloud as she went.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tamar puts ashes on her head, tears her garment, lays her hand on her head, and goes away crying aloud. These are signs of deep mourning.

Arminian readers honor her public grief as a true response to a grievous wrong.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tamar does not hide what has been done to her. Her lament is open.

Reformed readers see righteous grief, not shame on her part. Both traditions read her mourning with deep respect and as shared ground: the wrong was real, and her sorrow is fitting.

verses.text: Absalom her brother said to her, “Has Amnon your brother been with you? But now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother. Don’t take this thing to heart.” So Tamar remained desolate in her brother Absalom’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom asks whether Amnon has been with her, tells her to hold her peace because he is her brother, and Tamar remains desolate in his house. Her grief is silenced.

Arminian readers see Absalom’s ‘be quiet’ as a further failure to honor her voice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom shelters her but asks her to keep silent. ‘Desolate’ describes her lasting condition.

Reformed readers see protection mixed with suppression. Both traditions read this plainly, honoring Tamar’s desolation without excusing anyone who silenced her.

verses.text: But when King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.
verses.arminianNotes:
When David hears, he is very angry. The text reports no action.

Arminian readers name this as a real failure of justice. Anger without action left Tamar without redress and Amnon unpunished.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s anger is appropriate, but he does nothing. His own sin may have weakened his moral authority, though the text does not explain his inaction.

Reformed readers likewise see a failure that should not be excused. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with sobering consequences ahead.

verses.text: Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad; for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.
verses.arminianNotes:
Absalom says nothing good or bad to Amnon, for he hates him because he forced Tamar. Silence hides resentment.

Arminian readers see hatred being nursed rather than addressed through justice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Absalom’s silence is not peace. It conceals a purpose that will emerge later.

Reformed readers see how unaddressed sin breeds further sin in David’s house, as 12:10–12 foretold. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without treating Absalom’s hatred as righteous vengeance.
